thread.title: Can The Stock Market Stay On The Bull? The Test Is On | Investor's Business Daily

author: PAUL WHITFIELD
title: Can The Stock Market Stay On The Bull? The Test Is On | Investor's Business Daily
text:
The stock market was on track to exact revenge on the bears for a second day in a row. Bulls, though, have seen negative reversals wipe out early gains in some recent sessions.
X In late-morning trade Wednesday, the Nasdaq's thrust was at 1.9%. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones industrial average posted gains of 1.2% and 1.1% respectively.
Small caps lagged with the Russell 2000 up 0.8%.
Volume in the stock market fell on the NYSE but rose on the Nasdaq.

Four Bullish Items No. 1, the put/call ratio has surpassed the 1.5 level four times this month — Oct. 11, 18, 24 and Friday. When the secondary fear gauge reaches those levels, a market bottom is often near.
No. 2, Investors Intelligence's reading on bullish advisors vs. bearish advisors also could be pointing to a stock market upward bounce. The contrarian survey (fewer bullish advisors is bullish for stocks) took a bold step. The percentage of bulls fell to 44.3% from the previous reading of 50.5%. Early in October, the bulls were at 61.8%.
No. 3, the stock market itself is looking somewhat better from a technical aspect. Wednesday's gap up at the open oozed confidence. The previous four sessions involved two up days with high closes (Oct. 25 and Oct. 30), a down day that finished about 50% off the day's low (Oct. 26) and Monday's negative session. High closes are a bullish sign. Watch to see how the stock market indexes close today.
No. 4, on Wednesday the day's leadership was coming from quality groups — computer integrated systems, specialty consumer products and credit card companies. On the downside, defensive plays such as food, utilities and soap were taking hard hits.
Bulls like to see weakness among the defensive stocks because that presumably frees up money for more aggressive areas of the stock market.
Economic Data In financial news, ADP's national employment report for October trounced the Street's consensus estimate. Views called for 178,000 jobs added but came in 27% higher at 227,000.
The Chicago purchasing managers index for October came in at 58.4 vs. analysts' estimate for 60. Readings above 50 point to an expanding economy, while those below 50 suggest economic contraction.
The Energy Information Administration reported a 3.2 million barrel increase for the week in crude oil in the U.S. The price of West Texas Intermediate crude oil slipped 0.1% to $66.12 a barrel.
October's Scorecard October was a rough month for light sweet crude and stocks. The price of crude oil dropped about 10% for the month.
Stock market indexes were mostly down in October. According to preliminary data, losers included The Innovator IBD 50 Fund ( FFTY ), off 18%; the Sox semiconductor index, minus 13%; the Nasdaq, minus 11%; the small-cap S&P 600, minus 10%; the S&P 500, off 7%; and the Dow Jones industrial average, minus 6%.
One of America's most widely held stocks, Apple ( AAPL ), lost only 3% in October. Apple appears headed toward a 1.5% gain for the week, its first up week since late September. The megacap stock could be working on a flat base but needs to retake its 10-week moving average.
Winners included the Dow Jones utility average, up 3%; and the iShares Gold Trust ( IAU ), up 2%.
Among IBD's 197 industry groups, carmakers rose 21%; dairy, 12%; and tobacco, 5%. The biggest losers in October included mining and construction equipment, down 24%; internet retail, off 23%; and specialty steel, also minus 23%.
